text: Easing trait_cost_scale from 0.5 to 0.25. The tax was set to put a price on armour that had been free for two thousand eight hundred years, and it worked: prey defence has come from 1.47 down to about 1.25, comfortably under the genome ceiling of 1.60, and the niche reads open. But it has also taken this world from eleven living species to two, with Primordium vulgare at eighty-five per cent of all fauna, and the population from around 3,300 to somewhere near 1,200. That is the trade the README warned about in plain terms -- the same primary production supports far fewer animals once every trait costs upkeep, and small populations are demographically fragile. The job the tax was set is done, and at a small effective population size it stops being selection and starts being drift: armour was measured climbing back from 0.45 to 0.83 during the worst of the crash, which is the tax undoing its own work. A quarter keeps armour priced, so the ratchet cannot simply restart, at half the metabolic burden. If defence climbs back over about 1.4 it should go up again; if the species count does not recover within a few hundred years then the cost was structural rather than transitional and this world may need its primary production raised instead. Measured for reference: at growth_scale 0.13 and 0.19 the population held roughly 2,200 and 2,500 against 1,200 at the default, with armour 0.72 to 0.77 against 0.79 to 0.86. That lever is available and untried on the live world.
